newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan state utility stalls joint plan with China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan state utility stalls joint plan with China.

text.p: Taiwan's state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) has stalled plans for joint oil exploration with China following calls on the island to reduce economic ties with China, a company spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

The pact signed in July by the state-owned oil firms from the two archrivals had been seen as a breakthrough in Taiwan- China relations. Taiwan has banned all contact between its state firms and China since a civil war split the two sides in 1949.
The CPC spokeswoman said the joint oil exploration agreement with China had been stalled but declined to say whether the plan had been cancelled.
"We are a state company and we have to comply with the government's policy.
"It (the pact) is only a memorandum of understanding to show a willingness to cooperate by both sides, but not a concrete contract for investment," she told Reuters by telephone.

Under the landmark pact, CPC and Beijing's China National Offshore Corp agreed to conduct joint research and preparation for oil exploration between southern China's Pearl River delta and the Taiwan Strait.
The accord was put in the name of CPC's offshore subsidiary, Overseas Petroleum Investment Corp, to avoid violating Taiwan government restrictions.
"All we can say now is there is no contact at this moment and we do not plan to hold talks with the mainland side in the near future," the spokeswoman said.
Worried Taiwan may be putting all of its investment eggs in one basket, Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui said in August the island should review its policy of investing heavily in China.

More than 25,000 Taiwanese businesses have poured some US$20 billion into China since political tensions between the two longtime rivals began to thaw in the late 1980s, making Taiwan one of the largest sources of foreign investment in China.
Various government agencies, including the Economics Ministry and the Mainland Affairs Council, the island's top policymaking body toward China, made similar comments following Lee's remarks.

CPC said in October that it would halt new overseas investments temporarily in response to the Economics Ministry's call to strengthen local investments, although contracted projects would continue as planned.
"We are a state company and we have to comply with the government's policy," the spokeswoman said.
Relations between Taipei and Beijing have been icy since Lee made a private but high-profile visit to the United States in mid-1995.
China, which regards Taiwan as a Chinese province not entitled to foreign ties, angrily postponed all semi-official talks with Taipei after Lee's trip.
Both governments in Taipei and Beijing say they want reunification, but disagree on the terms.
